newsitem.title: UK: UK's SFO says Maxwell ruling weakens fraud trials.
newsitem.headline: UK's SFO says Maxwell ruling weakens fraud trials.

text.p: George Staple, director of Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO), said on Wednesday that the court ruling in the Maxwell case last week had weakened the system of trying people accused of major financial fraud.

"The position now is that in the most complex fraud cases the indictment will be split up to produce a series of manageable trials...but it is very unlikely that a second trial will ever take place," Staple told a London conference on combating financial crime.
"The full criminality is unlikely ever to come before a court, nor will the defendants. The system is thereby emasculated," Staple added.

Staple said the judge's ruling in the Maxwell case, which threw out a second trial against Kevin Maxwell, son of media tycoon Robert Maxwell who died in 1991, had made it clear that it would be "unusual" for a second trial to take place.

Kevin and his brother Ian were acquitted in January after an eight-month trial and Judge John Buckley said last Thursday that a second trial against Kevin would "serve no further public interest". He later recorded not guilty verdicts.
Staple said while the Maxwell ruling did not "necessarily mean that after an acquittal severed counts cannot be tried in a subsequent trial", it meant later trials were unlikely.
He said indictments had already been reduced to a "bare minimum" after directions in the Blue Arrow case.

The SFO decided to "sever" the counts in the Maxwell trials to make the case more jury-friendly. This policy was encouraged by the appeal court which had quashed the guilty verdicts in the notorious Blue Arrow case.

Staple said this had been at the forefront of the way the SFO planned its investigations and prosecutions. It has not "overloaded indictments" but has tried to "reflect in the charges sufficient criminality to enable juries, on the evidence, to convict with confidence".

But there would inevitably be cases with several principal defendants "which are so complex that it is impossible to reduce them to a point where the whole indictment against all the defendants can be tried in a single trial".
The Maxwell case was an example of this and had therefore been split up into several trials which, Staple said, were thought "to be fair and manageable before a separate jury".
But as a consequence, the first and subsequent trials would only go ahead on part of the available evidence and not all the defendants would be before the court in each case.
"The jury will never see the full weight of the case against all." he said.
Staple said it was not a question of whether juries can understand the cases and "still less is it a question of the decisions of juries not being accepted by the authorities...they are accepted".
He said the main question was whether it was reasonable to ask an ordinary jury to sit through the entire lengthy case and at the end of this process deliver a verdict.

"I said last week that the judgement in the Maxwell case had serious implications for the prosecution of the largest and most complex criminal cases. A solution to this problem is now urgently required," Staple concluded.
